sources.title: Robert Koch (English Wikipedia) -- orientation only; not used as support for any scored row. Korean Wikipedia title '로베르트 코흐' confirmed via the Wikidata kowiki sitelink.

Robert Koch (Q37193) -- verified live via wbgetentities (2026-10-03): en label 'Robert Koch', description 'German physician, bacteriologist (1843–1910)', de 'deutscher Mediziner und Mikrobiologe (1843–1910)', ko label '로베르트 코흐' (ko description '독일의 의사, 미생물학자 (1843~1910)'), P569 1843-12-11, P570 1910-05-27, P18 'Robert Koch.jpg', enwiki 'Robert Koch', kowiki '로베르트 코흐', dewiki 'Robert Koch'. Orientation only.

Christoph Gradmann, 'Robert Koch and the Pressures of Scientific Research: Tuberculosis and Tuberculin', Medical History 45 (2001), pp. 1-32 (Cambridge Core open PDF, DOI 10.1017/S0025727300000028), read in full (body text; footnotes skimmed) -- SCHOLAR, CRITICAL (historian of medicine, Heidelberg; works from the Robert Koch Institute archive and Koch's letters). Read: the eight months from Aug. 1881 to the 24 March 1882 lecture; methylene-blue/vesuvin double staining developed while trying to photograph the bacilli (per Loeffler's account); blood-serum medium, guinea-pig passage, 10-15 day growth criterion, inoculation series; Baumgarten's near-simultaneous identification and Koch's continued experiments into 1883; the unpublished failed photographs and the speculative 'spores'; the 1884 shift from naming disposition/heredity/social conditions (1882) to treating them as residual; failed attenuation and disinfectant-therapy trials with Gaffky (never published, ended 1886); the 1885-90 career break and 1 Dec. 1886 letter to Flügge ('it may well take years'); 1888 letter to Farbwerke Lucius & Brüning on dyes; the Aug. 1890 announcement, his reluctance to disclose composition (only under pressure c. Jan. 1891), the 'secret remedy', his own revenue estimate of several million marks a year and the commercial negotiations with Prussian officials, inability to show the 'cured' guinea pigs, patient deteriorations/deaths, development with only Pfuhl and Libbertz, first human testing on himself; Gradmann's verdict of self-deception from 'an unshakeable commitment to his previously developed explanatory framework', not simple fraud; Koch's continued faith in tuberculin (improved tuberculin 1897, faithful at least until 1901); the 1902 bovine/human non-identity claim noted as 'ill-fated'. The identity of the second early human test subject (a private-life detail) is NOT used.

Robert Koch, Nobel Lecture, 12 Dec. 1905, 'The Current State of the Struggle against Tuberculosis' (English text from Nobel Lectures, Physiology or Medicine 1901-1921), nobelprize.org, read in full -- SELF. Read: his statement that his early warnings about bacilli-laden sputum 'have been un-heeded'; reasoning from the Prussian, English and Stockholm mortality declines to his conviction that hospital accommodation of advanced cases 'contributed most'; the open/closed tuberculosis distinction; his restatement (with Schütz) that bovine tuberculosis can be dismissed as a human source, citing the Imperial Health Office re-examination; continued recommendation of tuberculin preparations in sanatoria; the programme of notification, free sputum testing, hospitals, sanatoria and welfare centres, and his view that compulsory isolation could be dispensed with.

K. A. H. Mörner, Presentation Speech for the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (10 Dec. 1905), and the Nobel Foundation's biographical note on Koch (from Nobel Lectures, Physiology or Medicine 1901-1921), nobelprize.org, both read in full -- INSTITUTIONAL (award body; laudatory). Used for achievement facts and dates: anthrax work 1876 and wound infections 1878 at Wollstein while a district medical officer; solid-medium/pure-culture methods; Imperial Health Office from 1880 with Loeffler and Gaffky; the 24 March 1882 lecture; leadership of the German Cholera Commission in Egypt and India 1883-84; Hygiene Institute chair 1885; Institute for Infectious Diseases 1891; tuberculin 1890 ('did not live up to what was hoped', per the speech) and new tuberculin; the 1901 London claim on human vs. bovine tuberculosis and the 'strong opposition' it met; later expeditions (rinderpest, malaria, plague, East Coast fever, sleeping sickness and atoxyl 1906-07). The prize was 'for his investigations and discoveries in relation to tuberculosis'. Supports no trait row on its own; the biographical note's anecdote about teaching himself to read at five and its 'methodical persistence' characterisation are NOT used.

E. Ray Lankester, 'The Truth about Koch's Cholera Germ', Pall Mall Gazette, 6 Oct. 1884, pp. 1-2 (Wellcome Library copy, archive.org b30476379, OCR full text), read in full -- NON-SELF, ADVERSARIAL CONTEMPORARY (British zoologist, Professor at University College London; writes amid Anglo-German rivalry and openly says English men of science felt 'a certain sense of shame' that Germany led the India work). Read: his praise of Koch's tuberculosis proof by pure culture and reinoculation and his view of Koch as 'a conscientious reporter of his observations' whose account was 'perfectly candid and convincing'; his complaint that Koch let the public be 'mystified' by press reports for months before publishing; his charge that the Sept. 1884 report made a 'dogmatic declaration' that the comma bacillus 'must and shall' be regarded as the cause although no inoculation had reproduced cholera; Timothy Lewis's claim that the organism matched a mouth spirillum; and his attribution of the haste to German-French rivalry ('a rival to the French investigator Pasteur'). Hostile and partly wrong in hindsight about the organism; used as contemporary adversarial evidence about Koch's evidentiary standard and assertiveness, not as fact about cholera.

'The Cholera Bacillus -- Koch's Reply to His Critics', Science vol. 4 no. 98 (19 Dec. 1884), pp. 554-555 (JSTOR Early Journal Content, archive.org jstor-1761175, OCR full text), read in full -- NON-SELF, CONTEMPORARY JOURNAL REPORT (unsigned editorial note) summarising Koch's reply in the Deutsche medicinische Wochenschrift no. 45 (1884). Read: Koch examined Finkler and Prior's own specimens and found they had not obtained pure cultures and that their organism differed in size, growth rate and culture form; he did not find the comma bacillus in three cases of cholera nostras; he reported reproducing a cholera-like disease in rabbits and guinea pigs by duodenal inoculation of a minute dose of pure culture; E. van Ermengen's independent confirmation (Belgium, Oct. 1884); a slide of pure culture sent to the journal 'put up and forwarded by Koch himself'.

George W. Lewis Jr., 'Ten Days in the Laboratory with Dr. Robert Koch, of Berlin: The Methods to be Employed in the Cultivation and Detection of the Comma Bacillus of Asiatic Cholera', Buffalo Medical and Surgical Journal, March 1885 (reprint, 15 pp., US National Library of Medicine copy, archive.org 101704288.nlm.nih.gov, OCR full text), read in full -- NON-SELF, FIRSTHAND PARTICIPANT (an American physician admitted to one of the government-funded ten-day cholera courses Koch ran in Berlin, Oct. 1884-Jan. 1885, for delegations of four to six physicians). Read: the course organisation under Koch's direct supervision with assistants from the Egypt/India commission; side-by-side cultivation of the comma bacillus with the Finkler-Prior bacillus, typhoid bacillus and micrococci, including mixed inoculation of one tube, 'to render stronger the contrast between them'; the step-by-step medium preparation, sterilisation and dilution-plate procedure taught. Mostly technical; low weight, used only for the teaching/method-transfer pattern.

Robert Koch, 'On the Present State of the Bacteriological Diagnosis of Cholera', 'Water-Filtration and Cholera' and 'The Cholera in Germany during the Winter of 1892-93' (Zeitschrift für Hygiene, 1893), English translation by George Duncan, Professor Koch on the Bacteriological Diagnosis of Cholera, Water-Filtration and Cholera, and the Cholera in Germany during the Winter of 1892-93 (Edinburgh: David Douglas / New York: Jenkins, 1894-95), with a prefatory note by W. T. Gairdner (Glasgow, 15 Oct. 1894); archive.org professorkochonb00koch (Countway Library copy), read by sections: Gairdner's foreword and translator's preface in full; diagnosis chapter on gelatine-plate errors and Finkler's bacteria (pp. 11-13); the Hamburg-Altona-Wandsbek comparison and the reply to the 'localists' (pp. 25-29); the Nietleben asylum filter investigation (pp. 33-37) -- SELF (Koch) plus a short NON-SELF foreword. Read: Koch's use of the Hamburg/Altona water-supply boundary as an experiment that 'performed itself on more than a hundred thousand human beings'; his personal checking of contrary claims about house connections ('on the basis of information received by myself in Altona and Hamburg'); his sharp, sarcastic reply to Pettenkofer ('the revered Herr Localist in his embarrassment'); the protocolled interview of the Nietleben filter attendant and his computation of filtration rates; his insistence that filtration protects only if managed as strictly as at Altona; dismissal of Finkler's bacteria as the product of 'egregious blunders'. Gairdner (non-self, admiring) notes that 'many persons in this country ... have little confidence in Professor Koch' after the tuberculin failure, and that some will not 'coincide with the highly controversial attitude of Dr Koch in rebutting the ideas of his opponents', while praising the 'firm and logical statement of his arguments'.

Robert Koch, 'A Further Communication on a Remedy for Tuberculosis' (Deutsche medizinische Wochenschrift, 14 Nov. 1890), English translation as reprinted in Nature 43 (20 Nov. 1890), pp. 66 ff. ('Dr. Koch on Tuberculosis', from the British Medical Journal supplement), archive.org paper-doi-10_1038_043066a0, OCR full text, read in full -- SELF. Read: he had intended to complete the research before publishing but 'too many accounts have reached the public'; 'As regards the origin and the preparation of the remedy I am unable to make any statement'; the investigations carried out under his direction by Libbertz and Pfuhl with patients supplied by Brieger, Levy, Fräntzel, Köhler and von Bergmann; the 1:1,500 guinea-pig/human sensitivity estimate; the reaction he observed 'after an injection made in my own upper arm'; claims that first-stage phthisis patients 'might be pronounced cured' within four to six weeks and 'phthisis in the beginning can be cured with certainty', with a footnote that no conclusive experience on lasting cure existed; an earnest warning against 'indiscriminate application'; his omission of statistics and case descriptions.

Friedrich Loeffler, Vorlesungen über die geschichtliche Entwickelung der Lehre von den Bacterien, Teil 1 (Leipzig: F. C. W. Vogel, 1887), archive.org vorlesungenberd00lfgoog (Google scan, German OCR), read by sections: Koch's 1876 anthrax work (pp. 168-175) and Koch's 1877 preparation/staining/photomicrography methods and the 1878 wound-infection study, including his adoption of the Abbe condenser (pp. 216-235) -- NON-SELF, INSIDER (Koch's assistant at the Imperial Health Office from 1880, co-discoverer of the diphtheria and glanders bacilli; an admiring pupil writing a technical history). Read: Koch's serial transmission of anthrax from mouse to mouse 'durch lange Reihen von Generationen' (longest series twenty mice); step-by-step observation of growth and spore formation in a drop of aqueous humour on a heated stage; germination of spores followed back to bacilli; controls showing that other spore-forming bacilli from putrefying matter or hay infusions did not produce inoculation anthrax; drying and wetting tests on bacilli vs. spores and his explanation of soil/pasture outbreaks; his 1877 cover-glass drying, aniline staining and photography so that pictures would be free of 'willkürlicher oder unwillkürlicher Entstellung'; photographic distinction of B. subtilis from B. anthracis (flagella, cut-off ends); his search ('nach langem Suchen') for an illumination apparatus ending with the Zeiss/Abbe condenser. Admiring tone ('jeder Irrthum war ausgeschlossen') discounted.

H. C. Ernst, 'Robert Koch (1843-1910)', memorial notice for a Foreign Honorary Member, Proceedings of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences 53 (1918), pp. 825-827 (JSTOR Early Journal Content, archive.org jstor-25130022), read in full -- NON-SELF, CONTEMPORARY COLLEAGUE (Harold C. Ernst, Harvard professor of bacteriology). Read: the Wollstein consulting room partly converted into a laboratory with photomicrographic apparatus and dark room; the 'bitter controversy with Pasteur'; the 1887 cholera report bearing 'the marks of painstaking research and great accuracy'; the 'forced circumstances surrounding the announcement' of tuberculin and the disappointment; his characterisation of Koch's 'patience, a strong will and great persistence', modest manner and clear diction early, and in later life 'a tendency to general and dogmatic statement, and a greater inclination to controversial methods than had been seen before'.

S. Adolphus Knopf, 'Robert Koch. In Memoriam', address of 28 May 1910 at the New York Post-Graduate Medical School, Medical Record (New York), 4 June 1910 (reprint, Wellcome copy, archive.org b30614971), read in full -- NON-SELF, ADMIRING ACQUAINTANCE (American tuberculosis physician who calls himself one of Koch's 'humble disciples' and had received letters from him). Read: the motto 'nunquam otiosus' on his first scientific paper; 'the thoroughness with which he discussed any subject, and the firmness with which he defended any theory or fact which he thought right'; his repeated government assignments to local epidemics. A eulogy delivered the day after his death; very low weight, used only as minor corroboration.

Robert Koch, 'Berichte über die Tätigkeit der zur Erforschung der Cholera im Jahre 1883 nach Ägypten und Indien entsandten Kommission' (official dispatches to State Secretary von Boetticher, Alexandria 17 Sept. 1883 to Calcutta 1884; Arbeiten aus dem Kaiserlichen Gesundheitsamte III, 1887), as reprinted in Gesammelte Werke von Robert Koch, ed. J. Schwalbe with G. Gaffky and E. Pfuhl, vol. II/1 (Leipzig: Thieme, 1912), pp. 1-19 (Wellcome/LSHTM copy, archive.org b21353207_0001, German OCR), read: the volume's table of contents and the Alexandria and first Calcutta dispatches (pp. 1-12) -- SELF (official reports). Read: arrival when the Egyptian epidemic was already declining; the specific bacilli found in the intestinal wall of all fresh cholera cases and absent in a post-cholera case and in other deaths; his explicit statement that coincidence 'noch nicht' proved causation and that the bacterial invasion might be secondary; that he had earlier set no value on the same finding in Indian material because of possible putrefaction; 50 mice brought from Berlin plus monkeys, dogs and hens fed and inoculated without any result; his request to extend the expedition to India, offering to lead it; in Calcutta, isolation in gelatine culture, detection in all cholera cases and absence in eight non-cholera corpses (pneumonia, dysentery, phthisis, kidney disease) and in animal intestines, and his conditional argument that exclusive occurrence would make the causal link hardly doubtful 'selbst wenn die Reproduktion der Krankheit an Tieren nicht gelingen sollte'.

Robert Koch, 'Über die Milzbrandimpfung. Eine Entgegnung auf den von Pasteur in Genf gehaltenen Vortrag' (Kassel/Berlin: Fischer, 1882), as reprinted in Gesammelte Werke von Robert Koch, vol. I (Leipzig: Thieme, 1912), pp. 207 ff. (Wellcome copy, archive.org b21463608_0001, German OCR), read by sections: the opening (pp. 207-209), the passages on the chicken-cooling experiment and on Pasteur's publication practice (pp. 212-214), and the closing assessment of the Packisch and Hungarian trials (pp. 224-226) -- SELF. Read: that at the Geneva hygiene congress (Sept. 1882) he limited himself to 'einen kurzen Protest' against Pasteur's 'persönlich' and 'gereizt' polemic and reserved a full written reply; his statement of method -- it is 'noch nicht bewiesen' that all infectious diseases are parasitic, so proof must be furnished case by case, starting with exhaustive microscopic study using every staining and sectioning technique; that he disputed not Pasteur's chicken-cooling fact but its interpretation, citing 'vielfache eigene Versuche' with other birds; his principle that whoever claims the scientific world's trust 'hat die Pflicht, die von ihm befolgten Methoden so zu veröffentlichen, daß ein jeder in den Stand gesetzt wird, jene Angaben auf ihre Richtigkeit zu prüfen', with his charge that Pasteur kept his attenuation methods secret and reported only favourable trial results (Packisch, Hungary); and his acknowledgement of Pasteur's 'bedeutenden Verdiensten'. A polemical text; used for Koch's own stated standards and conflict style, not as a judgement on Pasteur.

experimentation.rationale: [src_koch_loeffler_1887, src_koch_gradmann_2001, src_koch_science_1884, src_koch_cholera_reports_1883 | 1875-1884 | insider (Loeffler) + critical historian + contemporary journal + self] Repeated, deliberately designed experimental series. Anthrax, 1875-76 (Loeffler, his assistant from 1880): serial transmission from mouse to mouse over long chains (the longest twenty mice); growth and spore formation followed step by step in a drop of aqueous humour on a heated stage; spores germinated back to bacilli; controls showing that other spore-forming bacilli from putrefying matter and hay infusions did not produce inoculation anthrax; drying-and-wetting tests comparing bacilli with spores. Tuberculosis, Aug. 1881-1884 (Gradmann): extended inoculation series in guinea pigs and rabbits by injection, feeding and inhalation of pure cultures, with the induced disease compared microscopically with that produced by tuberculous tissue. Cholera reply, late 1884 (Science report of his paper): he examined Finkler and Prior's own specimens and reported reproducing a cholera-like disease by duodenal inoculation in rabbits and guinea pigs. His own Egypt dispatch (Sept. 1883) records 50 mice brought from Berlin plus monkeys, dogs and hens fed and inoculated without result, and reports the failure. Counter-evidence kept in view: Gradmann shows his tuberculosis pathology rested heavily on short-lived guinea pigs, which limited what his experiments could reveal (see analytical_rigor).

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_koch_loeffler_1887, src_koch_gradmann_2001, src_koch_cholera_1893, src_koch_ernst_1918, src_koch_lewis_1885 | 1877-1893 | insider + historian + self + colleague + course participant] Close tracking of small specifics across several separate pieces of work. 1877 methods (Loeffler): he complained that bacterial drawings were schematic and neglected size relations and developed cover-glass drying, aniline staining and photography so that images would be free of 'arbitrary or involuntary distortion'; using photographs he distinguished B. anthracis from the supposedly identical B. subtilis by flagella and cut-off ends, and searched at length for an illumination apparatus before adopting the Zeiss/Abbe condenser. Gradmann notes that double staining was itself developed while trying to photograph the tubercle bacilli. Nietleben asylum cholera, 1893 (self): he had the filter attendant's cleaning routine taken down as a protocol, reconstructed the filter construction and computed the filtration rate (170 mm per hour); in the same work he warned that gelatine plates must be held at 22 degrees within half a degree or cholera colonies mimic Finkler's bacteria. H. C. Ernst (1918) says the 1887 cholera report bore 'the marks of painstaking research and great accuracy'; Lewis (1885) describes the step-by-step culture course Koch supervised, with comparison organisms grown side by side. Several independent instances; held below 80 because the non-self witnesses are admiring or technical.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_koch_pasteur_reply_1882, src_koch_cholera_reports_1883, src_koch_loeffler_1887, src_koch_cholera_1893, src_koch_lankester_1884, src_koch_gradmann_2001, src_koch_tuberculin_1890 | 1876-1893 | self + insider + adversarial contemporary + critical historian] Genuinely mixed, scored as a moderate lean. For: in 1882 he wrote that it was 'not yet proven' that all infectious diseases were parasitic, so proof had to be furnished case by case (self); in his Alexandria dispatch of 17 Sept. 1883 he wrote that finding the bacilli in every fresh case did 'not yet' show they were the cause, that the invasion might be secondary, and that he had earlier set no value on the same finding in Indian material because of possible putrefaction; in Calcutta he checked eight non-cholera corpses and animal intestines as controls (self); his anthrax work included specificity controls (Loeffler); in 1893 he argued from the Hamburg-Altona water-supply boundary as a natural experiment and personally checked the claims about house connections (self; Gairdner praised the 'firm and logical statement'). Against: Lankester (Oct. 1884, hostile) conceded his observations were 'perfectly candid and convincing' but called the causal claim, made without any animal reproduction, a 'dogmatic declaration' -- and Koch's own Calcutta dispatch argued the link would be hardly doubtful 'even if' animal reproduction failed; Gradmann documents unsupported conclusions in 1884 (invisible 'spores', a single recovering dog) and, in 1890, the 1:1,500 guinea-pig/human sensitivity estimate, while Koch's own Nov. 1890 paper said early phthisis 'can be cured with certainty' before any evidence on lasting cure existed. Strong on method and controls, looser when interpreting results that fitted his framework.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_koch_ernst_1918, src_koch_loeffler_1887, src_koch_nobel_presentation, src_koch_cholera_reports_1883, src_koch_gradmann_2001 | 1872-1885 | colleague + insider + institutional + self + historian] As a busy district physician in Wollstein with no research post, he cut off half his consulting room for a laboratory with photomicrographic apparatus and a dark room (Ernst) and, prompted by anthrax in the local herds, 'set himself the task' of settling its cause (Loeffler); the Nobel Foundation note adds that he worked in his flat with equipment largely provided by himself. In Sept. 1883, finding the Egyptian epidemic already waning, he proposed that the commission continue in India, where cholera was still active, and offered to lead it (his own dispatch); he then asked by telegraph to move the work to Calcutta. In 1885 he tried to leave the Imperial Health Office for a state-funded research institute of his own (Gradmann; the plan failed). Several independent episodes; confidence moderate because the Wollstein accounts are admiring retellings.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_koch_ernst_1918, src_koch_nobel_presentation, src_koch_gradmann_2001 | 1872-1882 | colleague + institutional + historian] Working solutions built from limited means. At Wollstein he turned part of his consulting room into a laboratory and dark room (Ernst) and, per the Nobel Foundation note, used his flat as the laboratory, inoculated mice with home-made wooden slivers and grew anthrax bacilli in the aqueous humour of ox eyes. In the 1881-82 tuberculosis work (Gradmann) the bacillus grew only above 30 degrees, where his gelatine media liquefied, so he switched to coagulated blood serum; material from human corpses was too contaminated, so he used an intermediate guinea-pig passage to obtain clean starting material; and, per Loeffler's account as cited by Gradmann, the double-staining method came out of his attempts to photograph methylene-blue preparations. Two independent clusters of instances; the Wollstein details come partly from institutional and admiring retellings, so confidence stays in the 0.5s.

persistence.rationale: [src_koch_gradmann_2001, src_koch_ernst_1918, src_koch_knopf_1910 | 1882-1910 | critical historian + colleague + admiring eulogist] Gradmann documents tuberculosis as 'a lifelong and intensive study' with papers, lectures and reports almost until his death (including a late-1909 letter to Kolle on extensive experimental studies). After his attenuation and disinfectant-therapy trials with Gaffky failed (ended 1886, never published), he wrote to Flügge on 1 Dec. 1886 that he had resumed experimental work 'with all enthusiasm' on a task that 'may well take years', and by 1888 was testing aromatic dyes against pathogens (letter to Farbwerke Lucius & Brüning). H. C. Ernst's 1918 memorial names 'patience, a strong will and great persistence' among his characteristics, and Knopf (1910) recalls the motto 'nunquam otiosus' on his first paper. The same persistence fed the tuberculin episode, which is scored under belief_updating rather than here. Confidence capped because the explicit characterisations are memorial tributes.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_koch_gradmann_2001, src_koch_nobel_lecture, src_koch_nobel_presentation, src_koch_ernst_1918, src_koch_cholera_reports_1883 | 1884-1905 | critical historian + self + institutional + colleague] Slow to revise central positions when evidence went against them. Tuberculin: when it was shown in early 1891 that fresh tubercles formed at the edge of tuberculin-necrotised tissue, and patient deteriorations and deaths were reported, he did not reopen his framework; he presented an improved tuberculin in 1897 and 'remained faithful to his remedy at least until 1901' (Gradmann), and in his 1905 Nobel lecture he still recommended tuberculin preparations in sanatoria (self). Gradmann attributes the affair to 'an unshakeable commitment to his previously developed explanatory framework' and notes that Koch 'completely stepped out' of the debates that followed. Bovine tuberculosis: his 1901 claim that bovine tuberculosis could be dismissed as a human source 'met with strong opposition' (Nobel presentation speech, 1905, which also notes bovine-type bacilli had been found in humans more often than 1901 experience suggested), yet he restated it without qualification in his Nobel lecture. Ernst's 1918 memorial describes a later 'tendency to general and dogmatic statement'. Counterweight: in 1883-84 he moved from an explicitly undecided position to a conclusion only after new culture evidence (his own dispatches), and in 1890 he accepted that guinea-pig results did not transfer directly to humans. Scored low, not extreme.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_koch_pasteur_reply_1882, src_koch_science_1884, src_koch_cholera_1893, src_koch_nobel_presentation, src_koch_ernst_1918, src_koch_gradmann_2001 | 1882-1905 | self + contemporary journal + self with Gairdner's foreword + institutional + colleague + historian] Stayed in open, sharply worded disagreement with leading figures across two decades. Pasteur, 1882: after a brief protest at the Geneva congress he published a full written reply accusing Pasteur of withholding his methods and reporting only favourable trials (self; Gradmann calls it a 'vigorous debate', Ernst a 'bitter controversy'). Finkler and Prior, 1884: he examined their specimens and publicly rejected their claims (Science report); in 1893 he still called their bacteria the product of 'egregious blunders' (self). Pettenkofer and the 'localists', 1893: he answered with sarcasm ('the revered Herr Localist in his embarrassment') and called the soil theory's explanation an 'utter failure' (self); W. T. Gairdner's admiring 1894 foreword nonetheless warns that some readers would not share 'the highly controversial attitude of Dr Koch in rebutting the ideas of his opponents'. Bovine tuberculosis, 1901-05: he held his position against 'strong opposition' (Nobel presentation speech). Ernst (1918) notes 'a greater inclination to controversial methods' in later life. dual_edged: the same readiness to fight kept his methods in front of critics and hardened disputes that later went against him.

INDEPENDENT PERSPECTIVES: (1) Koch himself -- 1882 Pasteur reply, 1883-84 cholera dispatches, 1890 tuberculin paper, 1893 cholera papers, 1905 Nobel lecture -- ONE self perspective, never the sole support of a row; (2) Friedrich Loeffler, assistant from 1880 (insider, admiring technical history, 1887); (3) E. Ray Lankester, British zoologist (adversarial contemporary, 1884); (4) Science editorial note (contemporary journal, 1884); (5) G. W. Lewis, American course participant (firsthand, 1885; low weight); (6) W. T. Gairdner, Glasgow professor (admiring foreword, 1894, with explicit reservations); (7) H. C. Ernst, Harvard bacteriologist (colleague's memorial, 1918, with critical remarks on later dogmatism); (8) S. A. Knopf, New York physician and admirer (eulogy, 1910; very low weight); (9) Christoph Gradmann, historian of medicine (critical, archive-based scholarship, 2001). The Nobel presentation speech and biographical note are institutional and support achievements and dated facts only. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: Gradmann (tuberculosis laboratory methods, failed therapy trials, 1886 and 1888 letters, tuberculin secrecy and claims, continued faith to 1901, 1885 institute attempt), Loeffler (anthrax experiments, 1877 photography/staining, Abbe condenser), Lankester (cholera claim without animal reproduction), Science 1884 (examination of Finkler-Prior specimens, inoculation reports), Ernst (Wollstein laboratory; persistence; later dogmatism and controversy), Gairdner (controversial rebuttal style), Lewis (course organisation), Knopf (thoroughness, motto). EPISODE USE (no episode supports more than two rows): Wollstein laboratory set-up 1872-76 (Ernst, Nobel note, Loeffler) -> proactive_agency, resourcefulness; anthrax experimental programme 1875-76 (Loeffler) -> experimentation, analytical_rigor; 1877 staining/photomicrography and Abbe condenser (Loeffler) -> detail_orientation; tuberculosis laboratory work 1881-82 (Gradmann: inoculation series, serum medium, guinea-pig passage, double staining from photography attempts) -> experimentation, resourcefulness; 1884 interpretive claims (spores, recovering dog) (Gradmann) -> analytical_rigor (counter-evidence); Pasteur dispute 1882 (self) -> conflict_tolerance, analytical_rigor (stated case-by-case proof standard); cholera commission 1883-84 incl. Lankester's critique (self dispatches, Lankester) -> analytical_rigor, proactive_agency (India extension); reply to critics / Finkler-Prior 1884 (Science, self 1893) -> experimentation, conflict_tolerance; cholera courses 1884-85 (Lewis) -> detail_orientation; failed therapy trials 1883-86, 1886 Flügge letter, 1888 dye trials, lifelong TB work to 1909 (Gradmann) -> persistence; 1885 own-institute attempt (Gradmann) -> proactive_agency; tuberculin 1890-1901 (Gradmann, self 1890, self 1905) -> belief_updating, analytical_rigor (counter-evidence); Hamburg-Altona analysis and reply to Pettenkofer 1893 (self, Gairdner) -> analytical_rigor, conflict_tolerance; Nietleben filter investigation 1893 (self) -> detail_orientation; bovine tuberculosis 1901-05 (Nobel presentation speech, self 1905) -> belief_updating, conflict_tolerance; Ernst's and Knopf's characterisations -> persistence, conflict_tolerance, belief_updating, detail_orientation (corroboration only). ROWS CONSIDERED AND LEFT UNSCORED: risk_tolerance (premature tuberculin announcement, injection into his own arm, commercial plans -- one episode only, and Gradmann argues he believed the remedy worked, so the episode reads as overconfidence as much as risk-taking; omitted); independent_thinking (positions against Pasteur, Pettenkofer and on bovine tuberculosis are already used for conflict_tolerance and belief_updating; Gradmann shows his tuberculosis concept built on Villemin, Cohnheim and Klebs; omitted to avoid double counting); collaboration (team work with Loeffler, Gaffky and pupils versus personal TB work and a closed two-man tuberculin circle -- genuinely mixed, would sit at the midpoint); leadership_drive (commission leadership, institute directorships and courses are largely offices; the behavioural part is captured in proactive_agency); competitiveness, achievement_drive, impact_motivation, autonomy_need (motive claims -- Lankester's and Gradmann's references to rivalry with Pasteur, institutional ambition and expected revenues concern motives and pressures and are not scored); systems_abstraction (his general methodology and the Hamburg natural experiment were considered; evidence mostly institutional or self, omitted); discipline, deep_focus (only the 'nunquam otiosus' motto and memorial adjectives); curiosity, cross_domain_range (the later tropical expeditions were largely government assignments and were not read in detail); decisiveness, execution_speed (the eight months from Aug. 1881 to March 1882 are an outcome, and Gradmann notes experiments continued into 1883). EXCLUDED ON PURPOSE: his divorce and second marriage, the identity of the second person who first tested tuberculin (a private-life detail in Gradmann), his health, final illness and death circumstances -- read where they appeared, NOT used; the biographical note's anecdote about teaching himself to read at five; the sleeping-sickness campaign of 1906-07 and atoxyl dosing in East Africa (listed in the Nobel note and Gesammelte Werke contents; the reports and critical scholarship were not read for this profile, so the episode is not used for any row or editorial item; a future revision that uses it should treat it factually and with critical sources); honours; Lankester's and Gradmann's statements about motives (rivalry with Pasteur, financial and institutional pressures) are reported only as their interpretations in rationale/editorial, not scored. No 'father of bacteriology' or 'first' claim is made; the cholera vibrio had been described before 1883, and the editorial says only that Koch isolated it in pure culture and found it in every case examined. KNOWN LIMITS: Brock's standard biography was not available; much of the insider evidence is admiring (Loeffler, Knopf) and the self material is substantial, but the profile also rests on an adversarial contemporary (Lankester) and a critical, archive-based historian (Gradmann), which is why belief_updating and analytical_rigor are kept moderate/low and conflict_tolerance is dual_edged. Lankester was wrong in hindsight about the organism (the comma bacillus is the cholera agent); he is used only for Koch's evidentiary standard. The Science 1884 report of reproducing cholera in animals by duodenal inoculation is Koch's own claim relayed by a journal. All confidences are at or below 0.66 and all scores below 80.
